user_input: Why does self-attention let a Transformer model long-range dependencies better than an RNN?
retrieved_contexts:
["# The Transformer Architecture

The Transformer, introduced by Vaswani et al. in 2017, replaced recurrence and convolution with a mechanism called self-attention as the primary tool for modeling relationships between elements of a sequence. Prior architectures such as RNNs and LSTMs processed tokens one at a time, which limited parallelization during training and made it hard to model long-range dependencies because information had to pass through many sequential steps. The Transformer instead lets every token attend directly to every other token in a single layer, so relationships between distant words are captured in one hop rather than many.

A Transformer block is built from two sub-layers: multi-head self-attention and a position-wise feed-forward network, each wrapped with a residual connection and layer normalization. Multi-head attention runs several attention operations in parallel, each with its own learned projections of queries, keys, and values, so that different heads can specialize in different kinds of relationships (for example, one head might track subject-verb agreement while another tracks coreference). The outputs of all heads are concatenated and linearly projected back to the model's hidden dimension.", "Extending context length has required progress on several fronts. Positional encoding schemes that generalize better to lengths unseen during training — such as RoPE (rotary position embeddings) combined with scaling techniques that stretch or reinterpret position indices at inference time — let a model trained at one context length process meaningfully longer sequences without retraining from scratch, though usually with some quality degradation the further the extrapolation goes. Efficient attention implementations, especially FlashAttention, reduce the memory bandwidth cost of computing exact attention by restructuring the computation to avoid materializing the full attention matrix in slow GPU memory, which does not change attention's quadratic compute cost but substantially reduces its practical memory and wall-clock cost. And architectural variants such as sliding-window attention (each token only attends to a fixed-size local window of nearby tokens in most layers) or various sparse/linear attention schemes trade some ability to model arbitrary long-range interactions for sub-quadratic (or even linear) scaling in sequence length.", "Because self-attention has no inherent notion of token order, Transformers add positional information explicitly. The original paper used fixed sinusoidal positional encodings added to the input embeddings; later models introduced learned positional embeddings, relative position representations, and rotary position embeddings (RoPE), which encode position by rotating query and key vectors as a function of their position, improving extrapolation to longer sequences than seen during training.

The original architecture had an encoder stack and a decoder stack. The encoder produces contextualized representations of the input sequence, while the decoder generates output tokens autoregressively, attending both to previously generated tokens (via masked self-attention) and to the encoder's output (via cross-attention). Encoder-only models (like BERT) are well suited to understanding tasks such as classification and extraction, decoder-only models (like GPT-style LLMs) are well suited to open-ended generation, and encoder-decoder models (like T5) are used for sequence-to-sequence tasks such as translation and summarization.

The main computational cost of a Transformer is the self-attention operation, whose time and memory scale quadratically with sequence length because every token must be compared with every other token. This has motivated a large body of work on efficient attention variants (sparse attention, linear attention, sliding-window attention) and on systems-level optimizations such as FlashAttention, which restructures the attention computation to reduce memory reads and writes on the GPU without changing the mathematical result.", 'Causal (masked) self-attention is used in autoregressive decoders: a mask sets the attention score from position i to any position j > i to negative infinity before the softmax, so a token can only attend to itself and earlier tokens. This enforces that the model cannot "look ahead" at tokens it is supposed to predict, which is essential for training decoder-only language models with teacher forcing and for correct behavior during generation.

Attention weights are sometimes used for interpretability, on the intuition that high attention from token A to token B means B was influential in producing A's representation. This intuition is not fully reliable in deep, multi-layer, multi-head models, because information is mixed across many layers and heads and the residual stream carries forward information that never gets explicitly "re-attended" to. Attention weights are best treated as one diagnostic signal among several, not as a complete causal explanation of model behavior.

Key-value (KV) caching is an inference-time optimization for autoregressive decoding: since causal attention means past keys and values never change as new tokens are generated, they can be computed once and cached, so each new token only requires computing attention against the cached K/V pairs rather than recomputing them for the whole sequence. This is what makes token-by-token generation with large decoder-only models tractable in production.', '# Attention Mechanisms

Attention is a way for a model to compute a weighted combination of a set of values, where the weights are determined by how relevant each value is to a given query. In the scaled dot-product attention used by Transformers, every input token is projected into three vectors: a query (Q), a key (K), and a value (V). The attention score between a query and a key is their dot product, scaled by the square root of the key dimension to keep gradients stable, and then passed through a softmax so the scores for a given query sum to one. The output for that query is the weighted sum of all value vectors, using those softmax weights.

Self-attention is the special case where queries, keys, and values all come from the same sequence, so each token attends to every other token in that sequence, including itself. Cross-attention is the case where queries come from one sequence (for example, a decoder's partially generated output) and keys/values come from a different sequence (for example, an encoder's output), which is how encoder-decoder models condition generation on an input.

Multi-head attention splits the query, key, and value projections into several smaller subspaces ("heads"), runs scaled dot-product attention independently in each subspace, and concatenates the results. This lets the model attend to information from different representation subspaces at different positions simultaneously, rather than being forced to average all relevant signals into a single attention distribution per layer.']
response: Self-attention in Transformers allows modeling long-range dependencies more effectively because it enables every token to attend directly to every other token in a single layer, rather than information having to pass through many sequential steps as in Recurrent Neural Networks (RNNs). This direct access captures relationships between distant words in one hop, facilitating better capture of long-range dependencies.
reference: Self-attention lets every token attend directly to every other token in a single layer, so relationships between distant tokens are captured in one hop, whereas an RNN has to pass information through many sequential steps, which limits parallelization and makes long-range dependencies harder to model.

This has motivated a large body of work on efficient attention variants (sparse attention, linear attention, sliding-window attention) and on systems-level optimizations such as FlashAttention, which restructures the attention computation to reduce memory reads and writes on the GPU without changing the mathematical result.", '# Hallucination in Large Language Models

Hallucination refers to a language model generating content that is fluent and confident-sounding but factually incorrect, unsupported by any source, or internally inconsistent. It is a direct consequence of how these models are trained and how they generate text: a language model is fundamentally a next-token predictor optimized to produce plausible continuations, not a database with a built-in notion of "I don't actually know this," so when a prompt pushes the model toward a topic it has weak or no reliable knowledge about, it will typically still produce a fluent-sounding answer rather than an explicit admission of uncertainty, because fluent continuation is what the training objective rewards.

It is useful to distinguish two broad categories. Intrinsic hallucination happens when a model contradicts information that was actually given to it in its own context — for example, summarizing a document but inserting a detail the document never stated, or contradicting an instruction given earlier in the same conversation. Extrinsic hallucination happens when a model asserts something about the world that cannot be verified against, or is contradicted by, its provided context or reliable external sources — this is the more commonly discussed form, and it is what RAG's faithfulness metric specifically targets: does every claim in the answer trace back to something actually present in the retrieved context, or did the model add unsupported claims from its parametric memory?', "Quantization is not free: aggressive quantization (very low bit-widths, or quantizing without a good calibration process) can measurably degrade a model's reasoning ability, its faithfulness to long context, and its calibration (how well its confidence matches its actual accuracy), even when it still produces fluent-looking text — which is why quantized models used in production, especially as an LLM-as-judge in an evaluation pipeline, should be spot-checked against the full-precision model's outputs rather than assumed to be equivalent.", 'For RAG specifically, the RAGAS framework decomposes evaluation into metrics that isolate retrieval quality from generation quality, since a RAG system can fail at either stage independently. user_input: Why is cosine similarity generally preferred over raw dot product for comparing text embeddings?
retrieved_contexts:
['The most common way to compare two embeddings is cosine similarity, which measures the cosine of the angle between two vectors and ignores their magnitude — this is preferred over raw dot product or Euclidean distance for text embeddings because it makes similarity invariant to how "long" a document's embedding happens to be, which can vary with text length or encoder quirks. Many embedding models are explicitly trained so that cosine similarity between their outputs is a meaningful similarity score, and some libraries normalize embeddings to unit length so that cosine similarity and dot product become equivalent.

Embedding dimensionality is a practical trade-off: higher-dimensional embeddings (768, 1024, or more) can encode more nuanced distinctions but cost more to store and search over, while smaller embeddings (384 or less) are cheaper and faster but may lose some discriminative power. Techniques like Matryoshka Representation Learning train a single embedding model so that truncating its output vector to a shorter prefix still yields a usable (if slightly less accurate) embedding, letting one model serve multiple storage/accuracy trade-offs.

A common failure mode in retrieval systems is embedding models struggling with out-of-domain vocabulary — a general-purpose embedding model trained mostly on web text may not distinguish well between two sentences that differ only in specialized technical or legal terminology, because it never learned that those terms carry different meaning. This is one reason domain-specific fine-tuning, or combining semantic embeddings with lexical methods like BM25, often improves retrieval quality over semantic search alone.', '# Hybrid Search and Re-ranking

Hybrid search combines a sparse lexical method (typically BM25) with a dense semantic method (vector similarity over embeddings) into a single ranked result list, on the premise that the two methods have complementary strengths: BM25 is precise about exact terms but blind to paraphrase, while dense retrieval understands paraphrase and meaning but can miss queries that hinge on a specific rare term or identifier.

The central challenge in hybrid search is that BM25 scores and cosine-similarity scores live on different, incomparable scales — a BM25 score might range from 0 to 30 depending on the corpus, while cosine similarity is bounded between -1 and 1 — so the two rankings cannot simply be summed. Reciprocal Rank Fusion (RRF) sidesteps this by ignoring the raw scores entirely and combining rankings instead: for each document, RRF computes 1 / (k + rank) in each ranked list it appears in (where k is a small constant, commonly 60, that dampens the influence of very low ranks) and sums this across lists. A document ranked highly by either method gets a large contribution; a document that both methods agree is relevant gets contributions from both lists and rises to the top. RRF requires no score normalization and no tuned weights, which makes it a robust default, though a weighted linear combination of min-max-normalized scores is a common alternative when there is enough labeled data to tune the weights.', 'Sparse lexical retrieval has properties that complement dense semantic retrieval. It matches exact tokens, so it excels at queries containing specific identifiers, codes, product names, acronyms, or rare technical terms that an embedding model may not have learned to represent distinctly, since embedding models are trained on general semantic similarity and can conflate rare terms with semantically similar but distinct ones. Sparse retrieval also requires no model inference at index or query time (beyond tokenization), making it cheap, fast, and fully interpretable — you can always point to exactly which terms matched. Its weakness is the flip side of dense retrieval's strength: it cannot match a query to a relevant document that uses different words for the same concept (a query for "car" will not match a document that only says "automobile" unless the tokenizer or an explicit synonym list bridges the gap).

In practice, BM25 remains a strong and surprisingly competitive baseline in information retrieval benchmarks, and it is common for production hybrid search systems to run BM25 and dense vector search in parallel over the same corpus and combine their rankings, because the two methods tend to make different mistakes — errors are not perfectly correlated, so combining them recovers relevant results that either method alone would miss.', '# Embeddings and Vector Representations

An embedding is a mapping from a discrete or high-dimensional object — a word, a sentence, a document, an image — to a dense vector of real numbers in a lower-dimensional space, chosen so that geometric relationships in that space (distance, direction) reflect semantic relationships in the original data. The classic illustration is word2vec's observation that vector arithmetic on word embeddings can capture analogies, such as the vector for "king" minus "man" plus "woman" landing close to the vector for "queen."

Modern text embeddings are usually produced by encoder models trained with a contrastive objective: the model is trained so that embeddings of semantically similar texts (e.g., a question and its correct answer, or two paraphrases) are pulled close together in vector space, while embeddings of unrelated texts are pushed apart. Sentence-embedding models such as the Sentence-BERT family, E5, GTE, and BGE are trained this way on large collections of paired or weakly-paired text, often combining a general contrastive pretraining stage with task-specific fine-tuning (for example, fine-tuning specifically for retrieval).', "Semantic chunking uses embedding similarity to decide where to split: consecutive sentences are embedded, and a split point is inserted wherever the similarity between adjacent sentences drops sharply, on the theory that a sharp drop signals a topic change. Document-structure-aware chunking instead uses explicit structure already present in the source — markdown headers, HTML tags, PDF layout, or code function/class boundaries — to split along logical units the author already defined, which tends to produce the most coherent chunks when that structure is reliably present.

Chunk size itself is a trade-off along two axes. Larger chunks give the generator more surrounding context per retrieved chunk (fewer chances that a fact's necessary context got separated from the fact), but dilute the embedding: a long chunk covering several sub-topics gets one averaged embedding that may not closely match a query about any single sub-topic, hurting retrieval precision. Smaller chunks embed more precisely (an embedding of a focused, single-topic passage matches a focused query more closely) but risk fragmenting information that spans multiple sentences and increase the total number of vectors to index and search. A common mitigation is to embed and search over small chunks for precision, but expand each retrieved chunk to include its surrounding sentences or parent section before handing it to the generator, decoupling the unit of retrieval from the unit of context."]

user_input: What is the difference between HNSW and IVF indexes for approximate nearest neighbor search?
retrieved_contexts:
['# Vector Databases

A vector database is a data store optimized for indexing and querying high-dimensional embedding vectors by approximate similarity rather than exact match. Given a query vector, it returns the k stored vectors whose distance (commonly cosine distance, dot product, or Euclidean/L2 distance) to the query is smallest, using an index structure that avoids comparing the query against every stored vector — a brute-force scan that would otherwise cost O(n) per query.

The two dominant families of approximate nearest neighbor (ANN) indexes are graph-based and clustering/quantization-based. Graph-based indexes, most notably HNSW (Hierarchical Navigable Small World), build a multi-layer graph where each vector is a node connected to a small set of nearby neighbors; a query greedily walks the graph from an entry point toward closer and closer neighbors, giving very fast, high-recall search at the cost of higher memory usage and slower index build/insert times. Clustering-based indexes such as IVF (Inverted File Index) partition the vector space into clusters (via k-means) and, at query time, only search within the clusters closest to the query, trading some recall for lower memory and faster inserts; IVF is often combined with product quantization (IVFPQ) to compress vectors and shrink the index further.', "Indexing is central to query performance. A B-tree index (the default) is well suited to equality and range queries on ordered data and is what backs most primary keys and foreign keys. A GIN (Generalized Inverted Index) index is suited to data where a single column value contains multiple searchable elements — an array, a JSONB document, or the lexemes produced by full-text search — because it indexes each element separately and maps it back to the rows containing it, which is why Postgres's built-in full-text search (`tsvector`/`tsquery`) is typically backed by a GIN index. pgvector's HNSW and IVFFlat index types plug into this same general indexing framework, letting an approximate-nearest-neighbor vector index coexist with ordinary B-tree and GIN indexes on other columns of the same table.", 'pgvector is a PostgreSQL extension that adds a native `vector` column type plus distance operators (`<->` for L2, `<#>` for negative inner product, `<=>` for cosine distance) and index types (IVFFlat and HNSW) directly inside Postgres. ["# Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG)

Retrieval-Augmented Generation is an architecture that couples a language model with an external retrieval step: instead of relying solely on knowledge baked into the model's parameters during pretraining, the system first retrieves relevant passages from an external corpus and then conditions the model's generation on those retrieved passages, typically by inserting them into the prompt. First, hallucination: a model asked about facts it never saw, or saw rarely, during training will often generate plausible-sounding but incorrect text rather than admitting uncertainty; grounding generation in retrieved source text gives the model something concrete to draw from and gives users a way to verify claims against a cited source. Second, staleness: a model's knowledge is frozen at its training cutoff, while a retrieval corpus can be updated continuously without retraining the model. Third, cost and specificity: fine-tuning a large model to memorize a narrow, proprietary, or frequently-changing document set is expensive and often unnecessary if the same documents can simply be retrieved at query time.", "# Fine-Tuning, Prompt Engineering, and RAG: Choosing an Approach

Choosing between them is a question of what kind of adaptation is actually needed — a new skill or behavior, versus new knowledge, versus a narrow output format — and each has a different cost profile.

Prompt engineering adapts model behavior purely through the text of the input at inference time: instructions, examples (few-shot prompting), and formatting requirements, with no change to the model's weights. It is the cheapest and fastest option to iterate on, requires no training infrastructure, and works within a single API call, but it is bounded by the context window and by what the base model is already capable of — a prompt cannot teach a model facts it was never exposed to, and very long, complex instructions can be inconsistently followed by weaker models.", 'A common misconception is treating fine-tuning as a way to "teach the model new facts" as a substitute for retrieval: fine-tuning on a document corpus does tend to shift a model's outputs toward that corpus's style and can improve recall of frequently repeated facts, but it does not reliably give the model the ability to answer arbitrary questions about the corpus's long tail of specific details the way retrieval does, and it offers no way to cite a source or update a single fact without retraining. user_input: How does BM25 improve on plain TF-IDF?
retrieved_contexts:
['# BM25 and Sparse Retrieval

BM25 (Best Matching 25) is a ranking function used to score how well a document matches a query, based on the query terms that literally appear in the document — it is a "sparse" or lexical method, in contrast to "dense" methods that compare learned embedding vectors. BM25 is a refinement of the older TF-IDF (term frequency–inverse document frequency) family: it scores a document highly if it contains the query's terms frequently (term frequency), especially if those terms are rare across the whole corpus (inverse document frequency, which downweights common words like "the" that appear everywhere and carry little discriminative signal).

BM25 improves on plain TF-IDF with two adjustments. First, it saturates term frequency: the tenth occurrence of a query term in a document adds much less score than the second occurrence, controlled by a parameter k1, reflecting the intuition that a document mentioning a term ten times is not necessarily ten times more relevant than one mentioning it once. Second, it normalizes for document length using a parameter b: without this, longer documents would score higher simply by containing more words and thus more chances to match query terms, so BM25 penalizes term matches in documents that are much longer than the corpus average.', '# Hybrid Search and Re-ranking

The central challenge in hybrid search is that BM25 scores and cosine-similarity scores live on different, incomparable scales — a BM25 score might range from 0 to 30 depending on the corpus, while cosine similarity is bounded between -1 and 1 — so the two rankings cannot simply be summed. Reciprocal Rank Fusion (RRF) sidesteps this by ignoring the raw scores entirely and combining rankings instead: for each document, RRF computes 1 / (k + rank) in each ranked list it appears in (where k is a small constant, commonly 60, that dampens the influence of very low ranks) and sums this across lists. A document ranked highly by either method gets a large contribution; a document that both methods agree is relevant gets contributions from both lists and rises to the top. RRF requires no score normalization and no tuned weights, which makes it a robust default, though a weighted linear combination of min-max-normalized scores is a common alternative when there is enough labeled data to tune the weights.', 'Sparse lexical retrieval has properties that complement dense semantic retrieval. Sparse retrieval also requires no model inference at index or query time (beyond tokenization), making it cheap, fast, and fully interpretable — you can always point to exactly which terms matched. Its weakness is the flip side of dense retrieval's strength: it cannot match a query to a relevant document that uses different words for the same concept (a query for "car" will not match a document that only says "automobile" unless the tokenizer or an explicit synonym list bridges the gap).

In practice, BM25 remains a strong and surprisingly competitive baseline in information retrieval benchmarks, and it is common for production hybrid search systems to run BM25 and dense vector search in parallel over the same corpus and combine their rankings, because the two methods tend to make different mistakes — errors are not perfectly correlated, so combining them recovers relevant results that either method alone would miss.', 'Having a large context window does not guarantee a model uses all of it equally well. This staging exists because running the accurate-but-slow method over the entire corpus for every query would be too expensive, while running only the cheap-but-less-precise method risks passing lower-quality context to the generator."]

user_input: Why is chunk overlap used when splitting documents into fixed-size chunks?
retrieved_contexts:
["# Chunking Strategies for Retrieval

Chunking is the process of splitting source documents into smaller passages before embedding and indexing them, and it is one of the most under-appreciated levers in a RAG system's quality — even a perfect retriever and a perfect generator cannot produce a good answer if the relevant information was split across chunk boundaries in a way that neither chunk alone contains it.

Fixed-size chunking splits text every N tokens (or characters), optionally with an overlap between consecutive chunks so that content near a boundary still appears whole in at least one chunk. It is simple and predictable, and overlap (commonly 10-20% of the chunk size) directly mitigates the boundary problem, but fixed-size splitting is agnostic to the document's actual structure and can still cut a sentence or a table row in half.

Recursive character/token splitting improves on naive fixed-size splitting by trying a prioritized list of separators — paragraph breaks, then sentence breaks, then word breaks — recursively falling back to a smaller separator only when a chunk is still too large after splitting on a bigger one. This keeps chunks close to a target size while preferring to break at natural boundaries (like paragraph ends) rather than mid-sentence.", "Semantic chunking uses embedding similarity to decide where to split: consecutive sentences are embedded, and a split point is inserted wherever the similarity between adjacent sentences drops sharply, on the theory that a sharp drop signals a topic change. Document-structure-aware chunking instead uses explicit structure already present in the source — markdown headers, HTML tags, PDF layout, or code function/class boundaries — to split along logical units the author already defined, which tends to produce the most coherent chunks when that structure is reliably present.

Chunk size itself is a trade-off along two axes. Larger chunks give the generator more surrounding context per retrieved chunk (fewer chances that a fact's necessary context got separated from the fact), but dilute the embedding: a long chunk covering several sub-topics gets one averaged embedding that may not closely match a query about any single sub-topic, hurting retrieval precision. Smaller chunks embed more precisely (an embedding of a focused, single-topic passage matches a focused query more closely) but risk fragmenting information that spans multiple sentences and increase the total number of vectors to index and search. A common mitigation is to embed and search over small chunks for precision, but expand each retrieved chunk to include its surrounding sentences or parent section before handing it to the generator, decoupling the unit of retrieval from the unit of context.", "A typical RAG pipeline has an offline (indexing) path and an online (query) path. Offline, documents are split into chunks, each chunk is embedded, and the embeddings (plus the chunk text and metadata) are stored in a vector index. Online, an incoming query is embedded with the same model, the vector index returns the top-k most similar chunks, and those chunks are formatted into a prompt template along with the user's question and handed to the generator LLM, which produces an answer conditioned on that context.

The quality of a RAG system is bottlenecked by whichever stage performs worst: if retrieval fails to surface the passage that actually contains the answer, no amount of generation quality can recover, because the model was never given the right information. This is why RAG evaluation typically decomposes into retrieval metrics (did we find the right passages?) and generation metrics (given the passages we found, did the model produce a faithful, relevant answer?) rather than only scoring the final answer end-to-end.", 'Having a large context window does not guarantee a model uses all of it equally well. Empirically, many long-context models exhibit a "lost in the middle" pattern: retrieval accuracy for a fact placed near the beginning or end of a long context is measurably higher than for the same fact placed in the middle, even though the fact is technically present and attention in principle allows access to any position. This means simply having a large enough context window to fit all potentially relevant documents is not sufficient for a system to reliably use all of them — a RAG system with poor retrieval that dumps twenty marginally-relevant chunks into a long context is not necessarily better, and can be worse, than one that retrieves three highly-relevant chunks, because the model may fail to weight the genuinely relevant one appropriately amid the noise.

This is one of the more important practical relationships between RAG and long-context models: a bigger context window changes how many retrieved chunks can fit, but it does not remove the value of good retrieval and ranking — it is generally more reliable to retrieve fewer, more precisely relevant chunks (helped by good chunking, hybrid search, and re-ranking) than to rely on a large context window to compensate for imprecise retrieval by including many chunks and hoping the model finds the right one.', 'For RAG specifically, the RAGAS framework decomposes evaluation into metrics that isolate retrieval quality from generation quality, since a RAG system can fail at either stage independently. Context precision measures what fraction of the retrieved chunks are actually relevant to the question, penalizing a retriever that pads its results with irrelevant passages. Context recall measures whether the retrieved chunks, taken together, contain all the information present in a reference (ground-truth) answer, penalizing a retriever that missed something necessary. Faithfulness measures whether every claim in the generated answer is actually supported by the retrieved context, by decomposing the answer into individual claims and checking each one against the context — this specifically targets hallucination that happens even when relevant context was retrieved. Answer relevancy measures whether the generated answer actually addresses the question asked, independent of whether it is factually correct, catching cases where a model produces a well-supported but off-topic or evasive response.']

This helps maintain the coherence of sentences or other logical units across chunk boundaries, ensuring that relevant information for answering queries is not split between chunks.

user_input: When should you choose fine-tuning over RAG for adapting a language model?
retrieved_contexts:
['A common misconception is treating fine-tuning as a way to "teach the model new facts" as a substitute for retrieval: fine-tuning on a document corpus does tend to shift a model's outputs toward that corpus's style and can improve recall of frequently repeated facts, but it does not reliably give the model the ability to answer arbitrary questions about the corpus's long tail of specific details the way retrieval does, and it offers no way to cite a source or update a single fact without retraining. In practice, RAG and fine-tuning are complementary: a model might be fine-tuned to reliably follow a particular answer format or to better use retrieved context (sometimes called retrieval-aware fine-tuning), while still relying on RAG for up-to-date, citable factual grounding.', "# Fine-Tuning, Prompt Engineering, and RAG: Choosing an Approach

There are three broad ways to adapt a pretrained language model to a specific task or knowledge domain, and they are not mutually exclusive: prompt engineering, retrieval-augmented generation, and fine-tuning. Choosing between them is a question of what kind of adaptation is actually needed — a new skill or behavior, versus new knowledge, versus a narrow output format — and each has a different cost profile.

Prompt engineering adapts model behavior purely through the text of the input at inference time: instructions, examples (few-shot prompting), and formatting requirements, with no change to the model's weights. It is the cheapest and fastest option to iterate on, requires no training infrastructure, and works within a single API call, but it is bounded by the context window and by what the base model is already capable of — a prompt cannot teach a model facts it was never exposed to, and very long, complex instructions can be inconsistently followed by weaker models.", "Retrieval-augmented generation adapts the model's effective knowledge without touching its weights, by supplying relevant external information in-context at query time, as covered in the RAG document. It is the natural choice when the task is fundamentally about answering questions over a specific, possibly large or frequently changing, body of knowledge — because that knowledge can be updated by re-indexing documents, with no retraining required, and answers can be grounded in retrievable, citable sources.

Fine-tuning updates the model's weights on a task-specific dataset, so the adaptation is baked into the model itself rather than supplied at inference time. It is the right tool when the goal is to change how the model behaves — its tone, its output format, its ability to follow a domain-specific instruction schema, or a narrow skill like structured extraction — rather than what it knows. Full fine-tuning updates all of a model's parameters and is expensive in compute and data; parameter-efficient fine-tuning methods such as LoRA (Low-Rank Adaptation) instead freeze the original weights and train small, low-rank update matrices injected into specific layers, dramatically reducing the number of trainable parameters and the memory needed, at some cost in achievable adaptation capacity compared to full fine-tuning.", '# Evaluation Metrics for LLMs and RAG Systems

Evaluating a language model or a RAG system well requires different metrics depending on what stage of the pipeline is being measured, because a strong final answer requires several independent things to go right, and a single end-to-end score cannot tell you which one failed.

Classic NLP generation metrics like BLEU and ROUGE compare a generated text against a reference text based on overlapping n-grams (contiguous sequences of words). They are cheap to compute and require no model calls, but they penalize valid paraphrases that use different wording than the reference and reward superficial word overlap even when the meaning is wrong, which makes them a poor fit for evaluating open-ended, free-form answers from modern LLMs — two answers can be equally correct and share almost no n-grams, or share many n-grams while differing in a critical fact.', "# Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG)

Retrieval-Augmented Generation is an architecture that couples a language model with an external retrieval step: instead of relying solely on knowledge baked into the model's parameters during pretraining, the system first retrieves relevant passages from an external corpus and then conditions the model's generation on those retrieved passages, typically by inserting them into the prompt. The term was coined in a 2020 paper by Lewis et al., though the general idea of grounding generation in retrieved evidence predates that specific formulation.

RAG addresses three well-known weaknesses of relying on a language model's parametric knowledge alone. First, hallucination: a model asked about facts it never saw, or saw rarely, during training will often generate plausible-sounding but incorrect text rather than admitting uncertainty; grounding generation in retrieved source text gives the model something concrete to draw from and gives users a way to verify claims against a cited source. Second, staleness: a model's knowledge is frozen at its training cutoff, while a retrieval corpus can be updated continuously without retraining the model. Third, cost and specificity: fine-tuning a large model to memorize a narrow, proprietary, or frequently-changing document set is expensive and often unnecessary if the same documents can simply be retrieved at query time."]

user_input: What are the three stages of the classic RLHF pipeline?
retrieved_contexts:
['The classic RLHF pipeline has three stages. First, supervised fine-tuning (SFT): the pretrained base model is fine-tuned on a smaller, high-quality dataset of example prompts and ideal responses, written or curated by humans, to establish a baseline instruction-following behavior. Second, reward model training: human annotators are shown multiple model outputs for the same prompt and rank them by preference; this preference data trains a separate reward model to predict a scalar score for how much a human would like any given response. Third, reinforcement learning: the SFT model is further optimized (commonly with an algorithm called PPO, Proximal Policy Optimization) to generate outputs that the reward model scores highly, while a penalty term (typically a KL-divergence constraint against the original SFT model) discourages the policy from drifting so far that it starts exploiting quirks of the reward model rather than genuinely improving — a failure mode known as reward hacking.', '# RLHF and Alignment

Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback (RLHF) is a technique for adjusting a language model's behavior to better match human preferences, used after initial pretraining and supervised fine-tuning to make base language models into the helpful, instruction-following assistants deployed in production chat products. The core problem RLHF addresses is that "predict the next token" pretraining, and even instruction-tuning on example question-answer pairs, does not directly optimize for qualities humans actually want, like helpfulness, honesty, and harmlessness — those are properties of an entire response judged holistically, not something a token-level prediction loss captures directly.', "The typical production pipeline is therefore staged: a cheap, high-recall first stage (BM25 and/or dense retrieval, possibly fused with RRF) casts a wide net over the whole corpus, and a slower, high-precision second stage (cross-encoder re-ranking) refines the top candidates down to the small number of chunks that actually get passed into the generator's context window. This staging exists because running the accurate-but-slow method over the entire corpus for every query would be too expensive, while running only the cheap-but-less-precise method risks passing lower-quality context to the generator.", 'The classic formulation of distillation, introduced by Hinton et al., trains the student not just to match the teacher's single top prediction (a "hard label") but to match the teacher's full output probability distribution over all possible outputs (a "soft label"). The intuition is that a teacher's probability distribution carries more information than its single most likely answer — if a teacher assigns 70% probability to "cat" and 25% to "dog" and 5% to everything else for a given image, that relative ranking and those relative magnitudes convey which mistakes are "reasonable" (confusing cat and dog) versus "unreasonable" (confusing cat and truck), information a single hard label throws away. A temperature parameter is used to soften the teacher's distribution (making the non-top probabilities larger and more informative) before computing the training loss against the student.', "The connector module is where architectures diverge. A simple linear projection (or a small MLP) maps each patch embedding directly into the LLM's embedding dimension, preserving one token per image patch — simple and information-preserving, but it can produce a large number of visual tokens for a high-resolution image, consuming a significant fraction of the LLM's context window. Resampler-based connectors (such as the Q-Former used in BLIP-2, or the perceiver-resampler pattern) instead use a small set of learned query vectors that cross-attend into the full set of patch features and compress them down to a fixed, much smaller number of tokens regardless of image resolution, trading some spatial detail for a far more context-efficient representation.

user_input: What do the RAGAS metrics context precision and context recall each measure?
retrieved_contexts:
['For RAG specifically, the RAGAS framework decomposes evaluation into metrics that isolate retrieval quality from generation quality, since a RAG system can fail at either stage independently. Context precision measures what fraction of the retrieved chunks are actually relevant to the question, penalizing a retriever that pads its results with irrelevant passages. Context recall measures whether the retrieved chunks, taken together, contain all the information present in a reference (ground-truth) answer, penalizing a retriever that missed something necessary. Faithfulness measures whether every claim in the generated answer is actually supported by the retrieved context, by decomposing the answer into individual claims and checking each one against the context — this specifically targets hallucination that happens even when relevant context was retrieved. Answer relevancy measures whether the generated answer actually addresses the question asked, independent of whether it is factually correct, catching cases where a model produces a well-supported but off-topic or evasive response.', 'Because context precision and recall depend on knowing which chunks are truly relevant, and faithfulness/answer relevancy require judging semantic entailment, most RAGAS-style metrics are themselves computed by prompting an LLM judge with a decomposed, structured task (such as "list the individual factual claims in this answer") rather than by simple string matching, which means the reliability of these metrics is itself bounded by the judge model's own reasoning quality — a weak or inconsistent judge model will produce noisy metric scores, which is why the choice of judge model for an evaluation pipeline matters as much as the choice of the metrics themselves.', '# Evaluation Metrics for LLMs and RAG Systems

Evaluating a language model or a RAG system well requires different metrics depending on what stage of the pipeline is being measured, because a strong final answer requires several independent things to go right, and a single end-to-end score cannot tell you which one failed.

Classic NLP generation metrics like BLEU and ROUGE compare a generated text against a reference text based on overlapping n-grams (contiguous sequences of words). They are cheap to compute and require no model calls, but they penalize valid paraphrases that use different wording than the reference and reward superficial word overlap even when the meaning is wrong, which makes them a poor fit for evaluating open-ended, free-form answers from modern LLMs — two answers can be equally correct and share almost no n-grams, or share many n-grams while differing in a critical fact.', "A typical RAG pipeline has an offline (indexing) path and an online (query) path. Offline, documents are split into chunks, each chunk is embedded, and the embeddings (plus the chunk text and metadata) are stored in a vector index. Online, an incoming query is embedded with the same model, the vector index returns the top-k most similar chunks, and those chunks are formatted into a prompt template along with the user's question and handed to the generator LLM, which produces an answer conditioned on that context.

The quality of a RAG system is bottlenecked by whichever stage performs worst: if retrieval fails to surface the passage that actually contains the answer, no amount of generation quality can recover, because the model was never given the right information. This is why RAG evaluation typically decomposes into retrieval metrics (did we find the right passages?) and generation metrics (given the passages we found, did the model produce a faithful, relevant answer?) rather than only scoring the final answer end-to-end.", 'A common misconception is treating fine-tuning as a way to "teach the model new facts" as a substitute for retrieval: fine-tuning on a document corpus does tend to shift a model's outputs toward that corpus's style and can improve recall of frequently repeated facts, but it does not reliably give the model the ability to answer arbitrary questions about the corpus's long tail of specific details the way retrieval does, and it offers no way to cite a source or update a single fact without retraining. This is a particular concern for document and diagram understanding, where an incorrect but plausible-looking transcription of a label or a value is much harder for a downstream user to catch than an obviously wrong description of a photo.', 'Several factors increase hallucination risk. Long-tail or rarely-seen facts during pretraining are more likely to be misremembered or fabricated than well-represented, frequently-repeated facts. Long context windows can suffer from a "lost in the middle" effect, where information placed in the middle of a very long prompt is used less reliably than information near the beginning or end, increasing the chance the model ignores relevant retrieved context it was actually given. Ambiguous or underspecified questions invite the model to guess at the user's intent rather than asking for clarification. And instruction-tuned/RLHF'd models can develop a tendency toward sycophancy — producing an answer the model infers the user wants to hear, even when that conflicts with the evidence in context — which is a subtler form of unfaithfulness than outright factual fabrication.', 'Mitigations operate at different points in a system. This enforces that the model cannot "look ahead" at tokens it is supposed to predict, which is essential for training decoder-only language models with teacher forcing and for correct behavior during generation.

Attention weights are sometimes used for interpretability, on the intuition that high attention from token A to token B means B was influential in producing A's representation. This intuition is not fully reliable in deep, multi-layer, multi-head models, because information is mixed across many layers and heads and the residual stream carries forward information that never gets explicitly "re-attended" to. Attention weights are best treated as one diagnostic signal among several, not as a complete causal explanation of model behavior.

Key-value (KV) caching is an inference-time optimization for autoregressive decoding: since causal attention means past keys and values never change as new tokens are generated, they can be computed once and cached, so each new token only requires computing attention against the cached K/V pairs rather than recomputing them for the whole sequence. Hallucination refers to a language model generating content that is fluent and confident-sounding but factually incorrect, unsupported by any source, or internally inconsistent. user_input: In a vision-language model, what is the role of the connector module between the vision encoder and the language model?
retrieved_contexts:
["The connector module is where architectures diverge. A simple linear projection (or a small MLP) maps each patch embedding directly into the LLM's embedding dimension, preserving one token per image patch — simple and information-preserving, but it can produce a large number of visual tokens for a high-resolution image, consuming a significant fraction of the LLM's context window. Resampler-based connectors (such as the Q-Former used in BLIP-2, or the perceiver-resampler pattern) instead use a small set of learned query vectors that cross-attend into the full set of patch features and compress them down to a fixed, much smaller number of tokens regardless of image resolution, trading some spatial detail for a far more context-efficient representation.

Training a VLM typically proceeds in stages: first, only the connector module is trained (with the vision encoder and LLM both frozen) on large-scale image-caption pairs, to teach the connector to translate visual features into something the frozen LLM can already interpret; then, some or all of the LLM (and sometimes the vision encoder) is unfrozen and fine-tuned jointly on instruction-following, multi-turn visual dialogue, and task-specific data, so the model learns to actually follow visual instructions rather than just caption images.", "# Vision-Language Models

Vision-language models (VLMs) extend the capabilities of large language models to accept images as input alongside text, enabling tasks such as visual question answering, image captioning, document and diagram understanding, and grounding language in visual detail. Most modern VLMs share a common architectural pattern: a pretrained vision encoder converts an image into a sequence of visual features, a connector module projects those features into the same embedding space the language model expects, and the language model then processes the combined sequence of visual and text tokens using the same Transformer machinery used for text alone.

The vision encoder is typically a Vision Transformer (ViT), which treats an image as a grid of fixed-size patches (for example 16x16 pixels), linearly projects each patch into an embedding, and processes the sequence of patch embeddings with standard Transformer self-attention layers — the same way a text Transformer processes a sequence of word/token embeddings. Encoders like CLIP's vision tower are popular choices because they were pretrained with a contrastive objective against paired text captions, meaning their visual features already carry some alignment with language semantics before ever being connected to an LLM.", "# Fine-Tuning, Prompt Engineering, and RAG: Choosing an Approach

There are three broad ways to adapt a pretrained language model to a specific task or knowledge domain, and they are not mutually exclusive: prompt engineering, retrieval-augmented generation, and fine-tuning. Choosing between them is a question of what kind of adaptation is actually needed — a new skill or behavior, versus new knowledge, versus a narrow output format — and each has a different cost profile.

Prompt engineering adapts model behavior purely through the text of the input at inference time: instructions, examples (few-shot prompting), and formatting requirements, with no change to the model's weights. It is the cheapest and fastest option to iterate on, requires no training infrastructure, and works within a single API call, but it is bounded by the context window and by what the base model is already capable of — a prompt cannot teach a model facts it was never exposed to, and very long, complex instructions can be inconsistently followed by weaker models.", '# RLHF and Alignment

Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback (RLHF) is a technique for adjusting a language model's behavior to better match human preferences, used after initial pretraining and supervised fine-tuning to make base language models into the helpful, instruction-following assistants deployed in production chat products. The core problem RLHF addresses is that "predict the next token" pretraining, and even instruction-tuning on example question-answer pairs, does not directly optimize for qualities humans actually want, like helpfulness, honesty, and harmlessness — those are properties of an entire response judged holistically, not something a token-level prediction loss captures directly.', "# The Transformer Architecture

The Transformer, introduced by Vaswani et al. in 2017, replaced recurrence and convolution with a mechanism called self-attention as the primary tool for modeling relationships between elements of a sequence. Prior architectures such as RNNs and LSTMs processed tokens one at a time, which limited parallelization during training and made it hard to model long-range dependencies because information had to pass through many sequential steps. The Transformer instead lets every token attend directly to every other token in a single layer, so relationships between distant words are captured in one hop rather than many.

A Transformer block is built from two sub-layers: multi-head self-attention and a position-wise feed-forward network, each wrapped with a residual connection and layer normalization. Multi-head attention runs several attention operations in parallel, each with its own learned projections of queries, keys, and values, so that different heads can specialize in different kinds of relationships (for example, one head might track subject-verb agreement while another tracks coreference). The outputs of all heads are concatenated and linearly projected back to the model's hidden dimension."]

This allows the language model to process sequences combining both visual and text tokens using its standard Transformer machinery.
reference: The connector module projects the visual features produced by the vision encoder into the same embedding space the language model expects, so the language model can process the combined sequence of visual and text tokens using the same Transformer machinery used for text alone.

user_input: Why does LangGraph use an explicit state graph instead of a linear chain for agentic workflows?
retrieved_contexts:
['# LangGraph and Agentic Workflows

LangGraph is a library for building applications as explicit state machines (graphs) of nodes and edges, where each node is typically a function or an LLM call that reads and updates a shared state object, and edges determine what runs next. It was built by the LangChain team specifically to address a limitation of simpler "chain" abstractions (a fixed, linear sequence of steps): many real applications, especially agentic ones, need loops, conditional branching, and the ability to revisit earlier steps based on intermediate results, none of which a straight-line chain can express cleanly.

The central abstraction is the state graph: a developer defines a state schema (the shape of the data that flows through the graph — for example, a conversation history, a set of retrieved documents, a scratchpad of intermediate reasoning), adds nodes that each take the current state and return updates to it, and connects nodes with edges that can be conditional — a routing function inspects the current state and decides which node to execute next. This makes control flow explicit and inspectable: rather than an LLM implicitly deciding what to do next hidden inside a single large prompt, the possible transitions are declared upfront as edges in a graph, even if the routing decision at a particular edge is itself made by an LLM call.', 'LangGraph also provides built-in support for persistence (checkpointing the state graph so a long-running or multi-turn interaction can be paused and resumed later, potentially across process restarts) and for human-in-the-loop interrupts (a graph can pause execution at a designated node and wait for external approval or input before continuing — useful for agentic workflows where a proposed action, like sending an email or executing a database write, should be reviewed by a human before it actually happens). Both of these are naturally expressed as graph-level concerns — pausing at a node boundary and resuming from saved state — in a way that is harder to retrofit onto an implicit, single-prompt agent loop.

Compared to simpler single-prompt "ReAct"-style agents (where the tool-use loop lives entirely inside one long, repeatedly-appended prompt), an explicit graph makes the set of possible states and transitions easier to reason about, test, and debug — a developer can unit-test an individual node in isolation, or visualize the graph structure to audit what paths an agent could possibly take — at the cost of more upfront structure than simply writing a single prompt and letting the model figure out control flow implicitly.', 'This structure is well suited to agentic patterns where an LLM needs to take multiple actions and observe their results before responding: a node calls the LLM with the current state and a set of available tools, the LLM's response either contains a final answer or a request to call a specific tool, a conditional edge routes to a "tool execution" node if a tool was requested, that node runs the tool and appends its result to the state, and control loops back to the LLM node so it can decide what to do next given the new information — continuing until the LLM produces a final answer instead of a tool call. This explicit loop is what lets an agent perform multi-step tasks like "search for X, then use what you found to look up Y, then summarize both" without that entire procedure being hardcoded in advance.', 'For large language models specifically, distillation commonly takes the form of using a large, expensive model to generate a large dataset of high-quality outputs (answers, chain-of-thought reasoning traces, or preference judgments) for a wide variety of prompts, and then fine-tuning a smaller model on that generated dataset with ordinary supervised fine-tuning — sometimes called "sequence-level" or "black-box" distillation, since it only requires access to the teacher's text outputs rather than its internal probability distributions or weights, which is important when the teacher is only available behind an API. This is the approach used to produce many small, capable open-weight models that closely imitate the style and, to a significant extent, the capability of a much larger closed model on similar prompts.

Distillation has practical limits: a small student model has fundamentally less capacity than a large teacher, so it cannot perfectly replicate the teacher's behavior on the hardest tasks in the teacher's distribution, and a student trained heavily on a teacher's outputs can inherit the teacher's specific errors, stylistic quirks, and blind spots just as reliably as it inherits its strengths. Distilled models also tend to generalize somewhat less well outside the specific distribution of prompts they were distilled on, compared to a model of similar size trained directly on diverse human-generated data, which is why distillation datasets are usually constructed to be broad and diverse rather than narrowly focused on a single task.', "Communication between an MCP client and server happens over a small set of transport options — commonly standard input/output (stdio) for a server running as a local subprocess on the same machine, or HTTP (including support for streaming responses) for a server running remotely — with messages exchanged as JSON-RPC, a lightweight remote-procedure-call format built on JSON. Regardless of transport, the interaction pattern is the same: a client discovers what tools/resources/prompts a server offers (via a listing call), and then invokes specific tools or reads specific resources by name with structured arguments, receiving structured results back.

A practical benefit of standardizing this interface is composability: a single MCP server implementation for, say, a company's internal ticketing system, or a database, or a version control host, can be written once and then used by any MCP-compatible AI application — a chat assistant, an IDE integration, an autonomous agent — without that server needing to know anything about which specific application is calling it. This mirrors the earlier value proposition of the Language Server Protocol (LSP) in code editors, which let one language server (say, for Python) work with any LSP-compatible editor, instead of every editor needing its own bespoke Python language support."]

user_input: What are the three primitives an MCP server can expose?
retrieved_contexts:
["# Model Context Protocol (MCP)

The Model Context Protocol (MCP) is an open standard for connecting AI applications to external tools, data sources, and systems through a common client-server interface, rather than every AI application and every external system needing a bespoke, one-off integration. Before a shared protocol, connecting an LLM application to N different tools or data sources typically required writing N different custom integrations; MCP aims to turn this into an M-times-N problem into an M-plus-N problem, where any MCP-compatible client can talk to any MCP-compatible server without custom glue code for each pair.

An MCP server exposes some combination of three primitives. Tools are callable functions with a defined input schema that the AI model can invoke to take an action or fetch information (for example, running a database query, sending a message, or searching the web) — conceptually similar to function calling/tool use already supported by most LLM providers, but standardized so the same tool server works across different client applications. Resources are addressable pieces of data (files, database records, API responses) that a client can read and provide as context to the model, distinct from tools in that reading a resource is meant to be a side-effect-free retrieval rather than an action. Prompts are reusable, parameterized prompt templates that a server can expose so that common interaction patterns don't need to be re-authored in every client that wants to use that server.", "Communication between an MCP client and server happens over a small set of transport options — commonly standard input/output (stdio) for a server running as a local subprocess on the same machine, or HTTP (including support for streaming responses) for a server running remotely — with messages exchanged as JSON-RPC, a lightweight remote-procedure-call format built on JSON. Regardless of transport, the interaction pattern is the same: a client discovers what tools/resources/prompts a server offers (via a listing call), and then invokes specific tools or reads specific resources by name with structured arguments, receiving structured results back.

user_input: Why does Postgres use MVCC, and what operational concern does it create?
retrieved_contexts:
['# PostgreSQL Fundamentals Relevant to Search Systems

PostgreSQL is an open-source, object-relational database management system known for standards compliance, strong transactional guarantees (full ACID compliance), and an extension system that lets it take on capabilities well beyond a traditional row-store relational database, including full-text search, JSON document storage, geospatial data (via PostGIS), and, via pgvector, vector similarity search.

At the storage level, Postgres organizes data as rows within pages (typically 8KB blocks) within table files, and Postgres uses Multi-Version Concurrency Control (MVCC) to let readers and writers operate concurrently without blocking each other: rather than locking a row for the duration of a transaction, an update creates a new version of the row and marks the old version as no longer current for future transactions, while transactions already in progress continue to see the row version that was current when they started. This is why long-running transactions and un-vacuumed dead row versions ("bloat") are an operational concern — periodic vacuuming reclaims space from row versions no longer visible to any active transaction.', 'pgvector is a PostgreSQL extension that adds a native `vector` column type plus distance operators (`<->` for L2, `<#>` for negative inner product, `<=>` for cosine distance) and index types (IVFFlat and HNSW) directly inside Postgres. Its main appeal is operational: teams that already run Postgres get vector search without introducing a separate database system, can join vector search results against relational metadata in a single SQL query, and get transactional guarantees and existing backup/replication tooling for free. The trade-off compared to purpose-built vector databases (Pinecone, Weaviate, Qdrant, Milvus) is typically raw scale and some advanced features (e.g., very large-scale sharded search, some quantization schemes), though pgvector has closed much of that gap as it has matured.

Every ANN index trades recall (the fraction of true nearest neighbors actually returned) for speed and memory. Recall is tunable: HNSW exposes parameters like `ef_search` (how many candidates to explore during a query) and `m` (how many graph edges per node), while IVF exposes `nprobe` (how many clusters to search). Increasing these parameters raises recall and latency together; a common evaluation practice is to plot a recall-vs-queries-per-second curve and choose an operating point that meets a latency budget while maximizing recall.', 'A practical consequence of running vector search inside Postgres rather than a separate vector database is that a single SQL query can combine an ANN vector search with ordinary relational filtering and joins — for example, "find the 10 most semantically similar chunks to this query embedding, but only among documents owned by this user and tagged as published" — expressed as one query with a `WHERE` clause and an `ORDER BY embedding <=> query_vector LIMIT 10`, rather than requiring an application to query a vector database and a relational database separately and merge the results in application code. The trade-off is that the vector index shares the same server's resources (memory, CPU, I/O) with the rest of the application's relational workload, so a very large or very high-throughput vector search workload can be a reason to consider a dedicated vector database instead.

Connection handling matters for any application issuing many short-lived queries, including a retrieval service: opening a new physical Postgres connection is relatively expensive (it forks a new backend process per connection), so production systems typically use a connection pooler (such as PgBouncer, or a pool built into the application's database driver) to reuse a smaller number of physical connections across many logical client requests, rather than opening and closing a connection per query.', "Indexing is central to query performance. Retrieval augmentation reduces hallucination by giving the model something concrete to ground its answer in, but does not eliminate it, because a model can still ignore retrieved context or embellish beyond what it supports; explicit prompting to "only answer using the provided context, and say you don't know if the answer isn't present" measurably reduces (but does not fully prevent) ungrounded generation. Citation-generation, where the model is required to attribute specific claims to specific retrieved passages, makes unsupported claims easier for a human (or an automated faithfulness check) to spot, because a claim with no attached citation is a clear signal to scrutinize. This is achieved by an update creating a new version of the row instead of locking the row for the duration of the transaction. The operational concern created by this mechanism is "bloat" from un-vacuumed dead row versions, which requires periodic vacuuming to reclaim space.

user_input: How does knowledge distillation differ from quantization as a model compression technique?
retrieved_contexts:
['# Knowledge Distillation

Knowledge distillation is a technique for training a smaller "student" model to reproduce the behavior of a larger, more capable "teacher" model, with the goal of retaining as much of the teacher's quality as possible in a model that is cheaper and faster to run. user_input: What are the two sub-layers of a Transformer block, and how is each one wrapped?
retrieved_contexts:
["# The Transformer Architecture

The Transformer, introduced by Vaswani et al. in 2017, replaced recurrence and convolution with a mechanism called self-attention as the primary tool for modeling relationships between elements of a sequence. Prior architectures such as RNNs and LSTMs processed tokens one at a time, which limited parallelization during training and made it hard to model long-range dependencies because information had to pass through many sequential steps. The Transformer instead lets every token attend directly to every other token in a single layer, so relationships between distant words are captured in one hop rather than many.

A Transformer block is built from two sub-layers: multi-head self-attention and a position-wise feed-forward network, each wrapped with a residual connection and layer normalization. Multi-head attention runs several attention operations in parallel, each with its own learned projections of queries, keys, and values, so that different heads can specialize in different kinds of relationships (for example, one head might track subject-verb agreement while another tracks coreference). The outputs of all heads are concatenated and linearly projected back to the model's hidden dimension.", "# Vision-Language Models

Vision-language models (VLMs) extend the capabilities of large language models to accept images as input alongside text, enabling tasks such as visual question answering, image captioning, document and diagram understanding, and grounding language in visual detail. Most modern VLMs share a common architectural pattern: a pretrained vision encoder converts an image into a sequence of visual features, a connector module projects those features into the same embedding space the language model expects, and the language model then processes the combined sequence of visual and text tokens using the same Transformer machinery used for text alone.

The vision encoder is typically a Vision Transformer (ViT), which treats an image as a grid of fixed-size patches (for example 16x16 pixels), linearly projects each patch into an embedding, and processes the sequence of patch embeddings with standard Transformer self-attention layers — the same way a text Transformer processes a sequence of word/token embeddings. Encoders like CLIP's vision tower are popular choices because they were pretrained with a contrastive objective against paired text captions, meaning their visual features already carry some alignment with language semantics before ever being connected to an LLM.", "Semantic chunking uses embedding similarity to decide where to split: consecutive sentences are embedded, and a split point is inserted wherever the similarity between adjacent sentences drops sharply, on the theory that a sharp drop signals a topic change. Document-structure-aware chunking instead uses explicit structure already present in the source — markdown headers, HTML tags, PDF layout, or code function/class boundaries — to split along logical units the author already defined, which tends to produce the most coherent chunks when that structure is reliably present.

Chunk size itself is a trade-off along two axes. Larger chunks give the generator more surrounding context per retrieved chunk (fewer chances that a fact's necessary context got separated from the fact), but dilute the embedding: a long chunk covering several sub-topics gets one averaged embedding that may not closely match a query about any single sub-topic, hurting retrieval precision. Smaller chunks embed more precisely (an embedding of a focused, single-topic passage matches a focused query more closely) but risk fragmenting information that spans multiple sentences and increase the total number of vectors to index and search. A common mitigation is to embed and search over small chunks for precision, but expand each retrieved chunk to include its surrounding sentences or parent section before handing it to the generator, decoupling the unit of retrieval from the unit of context.", 'Causal (masked) self-attention is used in autoregressive decoders: a mask sets the attention score from position i to any position j > i to negative infinity before the softmax, so a token can only attend to itself and earlier tokens. This enforces that the model cannot "look ahead" at tokens it is supposed to predict, which is essential for training decoder-only language models with teacher forcing and for correct behavior during generation.

Attention weights are sometimes used for interpretability, on the intuition that high attention from token A to token B means B was influential in producing A's representation. This intuition is not fully reliable in deep, multi-layer, multi-head models, because information is mixed across many layers and heads and the residual stream carries forward information that never gets explicitly "re-attended" to. Attention weights are best treated as one diagnostic signal among several, not as a complete causal explanation of model behavior.

Key-value (KV) caching is an inference-time optimization for autoregressive decoding: since causal attention means past keys and values never change as new tokens are generated, they can be computed once and cached, so each new token only requires computing attention against the cached K/V pairs rather than recomputing them for the whole sequence. This is what makes token-by-token generation with large decoder-only models tractable in production.', "# Context Windows and Long-Context Models

A language model's context window is the maximum number of tokens (a token being roughly a word-piece — a whole word, part of a word, or punctuation) it can process in a single forward pass, spanning both the input prompt and the tokens generated so far.
