user_input: What is the word2vec example commonly used to illustrate embedding vector arithmetic?
retrieved_contexts:
['# Embeddings and Vector Representations

An embedding is a mapping from a discrete or high-dimensional object — a word, a sentence, a document, an image — to a dense vector of real numbers in a lower-dimensional space, chosen so that geometric relationships in that space (distance, direction) reflect semantic relationships in the original data. The classic illustration is word2vec's observation that vector arithmetic on word embeddings can capture analogies, such as the vector for "king" minus "man" plus "woman" landing close to the vector for "queen."

Modern text embeddings are usually produced by encoder models trained with a contrastive objective: the model is trained so that embeddings of semantically similar texts (e.g., a question and its correct answer, or two paraphrases) are pulled close together in vector space, while embeddings of unrelated texts are pushed apart. Sentence-embedding models such as the Sentence-BERT family, E5, GTE, and BGE are trained this way on large collections of paired or weakly-paired text, often combining a general contrastive pretraining stage with task-specific fine-tuning (for example, fine-tuning specifically for retrieval).', 'The most common way to compare two embeddings is cosine similarity, which measures the cosine of the angle between two vectors and ignores their magnitude — this is preferred over raw dot product or Euclidean distance for text embeddings because it makes similarity invariant to how "long" a document's embedding happens to be, which can vary with text length or encoder quirks. Many embedding models are explicitly trained so that cosine similarity between their outputs is a meaningful similarity score, and some libraries normalize embeddings to unit length so that cosine similarity and dot product become equivalent.

Embedding dimensionality is a practical trade-off: higher-dimensional embeddings (768, 1024, or more) can encode more nuanced distinctions but cost more to store and search over, while smaller embeddings (384 or less) are cheaper and faster but may lose some discriminative power. Techniques like Matryoshka Representation Learning train a single embedding model so that truncating its output vector to a shorter prefix still yields a usable (if slightly less accurate) embedding, letting one model serve multiple storage/accuracy trade-offs.

A common failure mode in retrieval systems is embedding models struggling with out-of-domain vocabulary — a general-purpose embedding model trained mostly on web text may not distinguish well between two sentences that differ only in specialized technical or legal terminology, because it never learned that those terms carry different meaning. This is one reason domain-specific fine-tuning, or combining semantic embeddings with lexical methods like BM25, often improves retrieval quality over semantic search alone.', "# Vision-Language Models

Vision-language models (VLMs) extend the capabilities of large language models to accept images as input alongside text, enabling tasks such as visual question answering, image captioning, document and diagram understanding, and grounding language in visual detail. Most modern VLMs share a common architectural pattern: a pretrained vision encoder converts an image into a sequence of visual features, a connector module projects those features into the same embedding space the language model expects, and the language model then processes the combined sequence of visual and text tokens using the same Transformer machinery used for text alone.

The vision encoder is typically a Vision Transformer (ViT), which treats an image as a grid of fixed-size patches (for example 16x16 pixels), linearly projects each patch into an embedding, and processes the sequence of patch embeddings with standard Transformer self-attention layers — the same way a text Transformer processes a sequence of word/token embeddings. Encoders like CLIP's vision tower are popular choices because they were pretrained with a contrastive objective against paired text captions, meaning their visual features already carry some alignment with language semantics before ever being connected to an LLM.", '# Vector Databases

A vector database is a data store optimized for indexing and querying high-dimensional embedding vectors by approximate similarity rather than exact match. Given a query vector, it returns the k stored vectors whose distance (commonly cosine distance, dot product, or Euclidean/L2 distance) to the query is smallest, using an index structure that avoids comparing the query against every stored vector — a brute-force scan that would otherwise cost O(n) per query.

The two dominant families of approximate nearest neighbor (ANN) indexes are graph-based and clustering/quantization-based. Graph-based indexes, most notably HNSW (Hierarchical Navigable Small World), build a multi-layer graph where each vector is a node connected to a small set of nearby neighbors; a query greedily walks the graph from an entry point toward closer and closer neighbors, giving very fast, high-recall search at the cost of higher memory usage and slower index build/insert times. Clustering-based indexes such as IVF (Inverted File Index) partition the vector space into clusters (via k-means) and, at query time, only search within the clusters closest to the query, trading some recall for lower memory and faster inserts; IVF is often combined with product quantization (IVFPQ) to compress vectors and shrink the index further.', "The connector module is where architectures diverge. Retrieval-Augmented Generation is an architecture that couples a language model with an external retrieval step: instead of relying solely on knowledge baked into the model's parameters during pretraining, the system first retrieves relevant passages from an external corpus and then conditions the model's generation on those retrieved passages, typically by inserting them into the prompt. The term was coined in a 2020 paper by Lewis et al., though the general idea of grounding generation in retrieved evidence predates that specific formulation.

RAG addresses three well-known weaknesses of relying on a language model's parametric knowledge alone. First, hallucination: a model asked about facts it never saw, or saw rarely, during training will often generate plausible-sounding but incorrect text rather than admitting uncertainty; grounding generation in retrieved source text gives the model something concrete to draw from and gives users a way to verify claims against a cited source. Second, staleness: a model's knowledge is frozen at its training cutoff, while a retrieval corpus can be updated continuously without retraining the model. Third, cost and specificity: fine-tuning a large model to memorize a narrow, proprietary, or frequently-changing document set is expensive and often unnecessary if the same documents can simply be retrieved at query time.", "A typical RAG pipeline has an offline (indexing) path and an online (query) path. Offline, documents are split into chunks, each chunk is embedded, and the embeddings (plus the chunk text and metadata) are stored in a vector index. Online, an incoming query is embedded with the same model, the vector index returns the top-k most similar chunks, and those chunks are formatted into a prompt template along with the user's question and handed to the generator LLM, which produces an answer conditioned on that context.

The quality of a RAG system is bottlenecked by whichever stage performs worst: if retrieval fails to surface the passage that actually contains the answer, no amount of generation quality can recover, because the model was never given the right information. This is why RAG evaluation typically decomposes into retrieval metrics (did we find the right passages?) and generation metrics (given the passages we found, did the model produce a faithful, relevant answer?) rather than only scoring the final answer end-to-end.", "# Fine-Tuning, Prompt Engineering, and RAG: Choosing an Approach

There are three broad ways to adapt a pretrained language model to a specific task or knowledge domain, and they are not mutually exclusive: prompt engineering, retrieval-augmented generation, and fine-tuning. Choosing between them is a question of what kind of adaptation is actually needed — a new skill or behavior, versus new knowledge, versus a narrow output format — and each has a different cost profile.

Prompt engineering adapts model behavior purely through the text of the input at inference time: instructions, examples (few-shot prompting), and formatting requirements, with no change to the model's weights. It is the cheapest and fastest option to iterate on, requires no training infrastructure, and works within a single API call, but it is bounded by the context window and by what the base model is already capable of — a prompt cannot teach a model facts it was never exposed to, and very long, complex instructions can be inconsistently followed by weaker models.", 'For RAG specifically, the RAGAS framework decomposes evaluation into metrics that isolate retrieval quality from generation quality, since a RAG system can fail at either stage independently. Context precision measures what fraction of the retrieved chunks are actually relevant to the question, penalizing a retriever that pads its results with irrelevant passages. Context recall measures whether the retrieved chunks, taken together, contain all the information present in a reference (ground-truth) answer, penalizing a retriever that missed something necessary. Faithfulness measures whether every claim in the generated answer is actually supported by the retrieved context, by decomposing the answer into individual claims and checking each one against the context — this specifically targets hallucination that happens even when relevant context was retrieved. Answer relevancy measures whether the generated answer actually addresses the question asked, independent of whether it is factually correct, catching cases where a model produces a well-supported but off-topic or evasive response.', 'Having a large context window does not guarantee a model uses all of it equally well. user_input: What role does inverse document frequency (IDF) play in BM25 scoring?
retrieved_contexts:
['# BM25 and Sparse Retrieval

BM25 (Best Matching 25) is a ranking function used to score how well a document matches a query, based on the query terms that literally appear in the document — it is a "sparse" or lexical method, in contrast to "dense" methods that compare learned embedding vectors. BM25 is a refinement of the older TF-IDF (term frequency–inverse document frequency) family: it scores a document highly if it contains the query's terms frequently (term frequency), especially if those terms are rare across the whole corpus (inverse document frequency, which downweights common words like "the" that appear everywhere and carry little discriminative signal).

BM25 improves on plain TF-IDF with two adjustments. First, it saturates term frequency: the tenth occurrence of a query term in a document adds much less score than the second occurrence, controlled by a parameter k1, reflecting the intuition that a document mentioning a term ten times is not necessarily ten times more relevant than one mentioning it once. Second, it normalizes for document length using a parameter b: without this, longer documents would score higher simply by containing more words and thus more chances to match query terms, so BM25 penalizes term matches in documents that are much longer than the corpus average.', '# Hybrid Search and Re-ranking

Hybrid search combines a sparse lexical method (typically BM25) with a dense semantic method (vector similarity over embeddings) into a single ranked result list, on the premise that the two methods have complementary strengths: BM25 is precise about exact terms but blind to paraphrase, while dense retrieval understands paraphrase and meaning but can miss queries that hinge on a specific rare term or identifier.

The central challenge in hybrid search is that BM25 scores and cosine-similarity scores live on different, incomparable scales — a BM25 score might range from 0 to 30 depending on the corpus, while cosine similarity is bounded between -1 and 1 — so the two rankings cannot simply be summed. Reciprocal Rank Fusion (RRF) sidesteps this by ignoring the raw scores entirely and combining rankings instead: for each document, RRF computes 1 / (k + rank) in each ranked list it appears in (where k is a small constant, commonly 60, that dampens the influence of very low ranks) and sums this across lists. A document ranked highly by either method gets a large contribution; a document that both methods agree is relevant gets contributions from both lists and rises to the top. RRF requires no score normalization and no tuned weights, which makes it a robust default, though a weighted linear combination of min-max-normalized scores is a common alternative when there is enough labeled data to tune the weights.', 'Sparse lexical retrieval has properties that complement dense semantic retrieval. It matches exact tokens, so it excels at queries containing specific identifiers, codes, product names, acronyms, or rare technical terms that an embedding model may not have learned to represent distinctly, since embedding models are trained on general semantic similarity and can conflate rare terms with semantically similar but distinct ones. Sparse retrieval also requires no model inference at index or query time (beyond tokenization), making it cheap, fast, and fully interpretable — you can always point to exactly which terms matched. Its weakness is the flip side of dense retrieval's strength: it cannot match a query to a relevant document that uses different words for the same concept (a query for "car" will not match a document that only says "automobile" unless the tokenizer or an explicit synonym list bridges the gap).

In practice, BM25 remains a strong and surprisingly competitive baseline in information retrieval benchmarks, and it is common for production hybrid search systems to run BM25 and dense vector search in parallel over the same corpus and combine their rankings, because the two methods tend to make different mistakes — errors are not perfectly correlated, so combining them recovers relevant results that either method alone would miss.', 'A common misconception is treating fine-tuning as a way to "teach the model new facts" as a substitute for retrieval: fine-tuning on a document corpus does tend to shift a model's outputs toward that corpus's style and can improve recall of frequently repeated facts, but it does not reliably give the model the ability to answer arbitrary questions about the corpus's long tail of specific details the way retrieval does, and it offers no way to cite a source or update a single fact without retraining. In practice, RAG and fine-tuning are complementary: a model might be fine-tuned to reliably follow a particular answer format or to better use retrieved context (sometimes called retrieval-aware fine-tuning), while still relying on RAG for up-to-date, citable factual grounding.', "A typical RAG pipeline has an offline (indexing) path and an online (query) path. Offline, documents are split into chunks, each chunk is embedded, and the embeddings (plus the chunk text and metadata) are stored in a vector index. Online, an incoming query is embedded with the same model, the vector index returns the top-k most similar chunks, and those chunks are formatted into a prompt template along with the user's question and handed to the generator LLM, which produces an answer conditioned on that context.

The quality of a RAG system is bottlenecked by whichever stage performs worst: if retrieval fails to surface the passage that actually contains the answer, no amount of generation quality can recover, because the model was never given the right information. This is why RAG evaluation typically decomposes into retrieval metrics (did we find the right passages?) and generation metrics (given the passages we found, did the model produce a faithful, relevant answer?) rather than only scoring the final answer end-to-end."]

This is part of the "term frequency–inverse document frequency" family that BM25 refines upon, ensuring that terms which are rare across the whole corpus carry more discriminative signal and thus contribute more to the score if they appear in a document matching a query.

This enforces that the model cannot "look ahead" at tokens it is supposed to predict, which is essential for training decoder-only language models with teacher forcing and for correct behavior during generation.

Attention weights are sometimes used for interpretability, on the intuition that high attention from token A to token B means B was influential in producing A's representation. This intuition is not fully reliable in deep, multi-layer, multi-head models, because information is mixed across many layers and heads and the residual stream carries forward information that never gets explicitly "re-attended" to. Attention weights are best treated as one diagnostic signal among several, not as a complete causal explanation of model behavior.

Key-value (KV) caching is an inference-time optimization for autoregressive decoding: since causal attention means past keys and values never change as new tokens are generated, they can be computed once and cached, so each new token only requires computing attention against the cached K/V pairs rather than recomputing them for the whole sequence. This is what makes token-by-token generation with large decoder-only models tractable in production.', "Communication between an MCP client and server happens over a small set of transport options — commonly standard input/output (stdio) for a server running as a local subprocess on the same machine, or HTTP (including support for streaming responses) for a server running remotely — with messages exchanged as JSON-RPC, a lightweight remote-procedure-call format built on JSON. Regardless of transport, the interaction pattern is the same: a client discovers what tools/resources/prompts a server offers (via a listing call), and then invokes specific tools or reads specific resources by name with structured arguments, receiving structured results back.

A practical benefit of standardizing this interface is composability: a single MCP server implementation for, say, a company's internal ticketing system, or a database, or a version control host, can be written once and then used by any MCP-compatible AI application — a chat assistant, an IDE integration, an autonomous agent — without that server needing to know anything about which specific application is calling it. Hybrid search combines a sparse lexical method (typically BM25) with a dense semantic method (vector similarity over embeddings) into a single ranked result list, on the premise that the two methods have complementary strengths: BM25 is precise about exact terms but blind to paraphrase, while dense retrieval understands paraphrase and meaning but can miss queries that hinge on a specific rare term or identifier.

The central challenge in hybrid search is that BM25 scores and cosine-similarity scores live on different, incomparable scales — a BM25 score might range from 0 to 30 depending on the corpus, while cosine similarity is bounded between -1 and 1 — so the two rankings cannot simply be summed. Reciprocal Rank Fusion (RRF) sidesteps this by ignoring the raw scores entirely and combining rankings instead: for each document, RRF computes 1 / (k + rank) in each ranked list it appears in (where k is a small constant, commonly 60, that dampens the influence of very low ranks) and sums this across lists. A document ranked highly by either method gets a large contribution; a document that both methods agree is relevant gets contributions from both lists and rises to the top. RRF requires no score normalization and no tuned weights, which makes it a robust default, though a weighted linear combination of min-max-normalized scores is a common alternative when there is enough labeled data to tune the weights.', 'Common failure modes include: retrieving passages that are topically related but do not actually answer the question (leading to a plausible but wrong answer); retrieving the right passage but having the generator ignore it in favor of its own parametric knowledge; retrieving too many or too few chunks, either diluting the context with irrelevant text or omitting necessary information; and the generator "hallucinating" a synthesis that goes beyond what the retrieved context actually supports, which is why faithfulness (does the answer only make claims supported by the retrieved context?) is tracked as a distinct metric from correctness. More advanced variants extend the basic pattern: query rewriting or decomposition before retrieval, iterative or multi-hop retrieval where the model retrieves, reasons, and retrieves again, and re-ranking retrieved candidates with a more expensive cross-encoder model before generation.', 'The most common way to compare two embeddings is cosine similarity, which measures the cosine of the angle between two vectors and ignores their magnitude — this is preferred over raw dot product or Euclidean distance for text embeddings because it makes similarity invariant to how "long" a document's embedding happens to be, which can vary with text length or encoder quirks. Many embedding models are explicitly trained so that cosine similarity between their outputs is a meaningful similarity score, and some libraries normalize embeddings to unit length so that cosine similarity and dot product become equivalent.

Embedding dimensionality is a practical trade-off: higher-dimensional embeddings (768, 1024, or more) can encode more nuanced distinctions but cost more to store and search over, while smaller embeddings (384 or less) are cheaper and faster but may lose some discriminative power. Techniques like Matryoshka Representation Learning train a single embedding model so that truncating its output vector to a shorter prefix still yields a usable (if slightly less accurate) embedding, letting one model serve multiple storage/accuracy trade-offs.

A common failure mode in retrieval systems is embedding models struggling with out-of-domain vocabulary — a general-purpose embedding model trained mostly on web text may not distinguish well between two sentences that differ only in specialized technical or legal terminology, because it never learned that those terms carry different meaning. This is one reason domain-specific fine-tuning, or combining semantic embeddings with lexical methods like BM25, often improves retrieval quality over semantic search alone.', "The typical production pipeline is therefore staged: a cheap, high-recall first stage (BM25 and/or dense retrieval, possibly fused with RRF) casts a wide net over the whole corpus, and a slower, high-precision second stage (cross-encoder re-ranking) refines the top candidates down to the small number of chunks that actually get passed into the generator's context window. retrieved_contexts:
['Re-ranking is a separate, typically later stage: after an initial retriever (BM25, dense, or hybrid) narrows a large corpus down to a small candidate set — say, the top 50 or 100 — a more expensive model re-scores just those candidates against the query and re-sorts them, before the top few are passed to the generator. Cross-encoders are too slow to run over an entire corpus (they require one full forward pass per query-document pair), which is exactly why they are reserved for re-ranking a short candidate list rather than for first-stage retrieval.', "The typical production pipeline is therefore staged: a cheap, high-recall first stage (BM25 and/or dense retrieval, possibly fused with RRF) casts a wide net over the whole corpus, and a slower, high-precision second stage (cross-encoder re-ranking) refines the top candidates down to the small number of chunks that actually get passed into the generator's context window. This staging exists because running the accurate-but-slow method over the entire corpus for every query would be too expensive, while running only the cheap-but-less-precise method risks passing lower-quality context to the generator.", 'Sparse lexical retrieval has properties that complement dense semantic retrieval. Sparse retrieval also requires no model inference at index or query time (beyond tokenization), making it cheap, fast, and fully interpretable — you can always point to exactly which terms matched. Its weakness is the flip side of dense retrieval's strength: it cannot match a query to a relevant document that uses different words for the same concept (a query for "car" will not match a document that only says "automobile" unless the tokenizer or an explicit synonym list bridges the gap).

In practice, BM25 remains a strong and surprisingly competitive baseline in information retrieval benchmarks, and it is common for production hybrid search systems to run BM25 and dense vector search in parallel over the same corpus and combine their rankings, because the two methods tend to make different mistakes — errors are not perfectly correlated, so combining them recovers relevant results that either method alone would miss.', "A typical RAG pipeline has an offline (indexing) path and an online (query) path. Offline, documents are split into chunks, each chunk is embedded, and the embeddings (plus the chunk text and metadata) are stored in a vector index. Online, an incoming query is embedded with the same model, the vector index returns the top-k most similar chunks, and those chunks are formatted into a prompt template along with the user's question and handed to the generator LLM, which produces an answer conditioned on that context.

The term was coined in a 2020 paper by Lewis et al., though the general idea of grounding generation in retrieved evidence predates that specific formulation.

RAG addresses three well-known weaknesses of relying on a language model's parametric knowledge alone. First, hallucination: a model asked about facts it never saw, or saw rarely, during training will often generate plausible-sounding but incorrect text rather than admitting uncertainty; grounding generation in retrieved source text gives the model something concrete to draw from and gives users a way to verify claims against a cited source. Second, staleness: a model's knowledge is frozen at its training cutoff, while a retrieval corpus can be updated continuously without retraining the model. Third, cost and specificity: fine-tuning a large model to memorize a narrow, proprietary, or frequently-changing document set is expensive and often unnecessary if the same documents can simply be retrieved at query time."]

user_input: What is the key difference between fixed-size chunking and recursive character/token splitting?
retrieved_contexts:
["# Chunking Strategies for Retrieval

Chunking is the process of splitting source documents into smaller passages before embedding and indexing them, and it is one of the most under-appreciated levers in a RAG system's quality — even a perfect retriever and a perfect generator cannot produce a good answer if the relevant information was split across chunk boundaries in a way that neither chunk alone contains it.

Fixed-size chunking splits text every N tokens (or characters), optionally with an overlap between consecutive chunks so that content near a boundary still appears whole in at least one chunk. It is simple and predictable, and overlap (commonly 10-20% of the chunk size) directly mitigates the boundary problem, but fixed-size splitting is agnostic to the document's actual structure and can still cut a sentence or a table row in half.

Recursive character/token splitting improves on naive fixed-size splitting by trying a prioritized list of separators — paragraph breaks, then sentence breaks, then word breaks — recursively falling back to a smaller separator only when a chunk is still too large after splitting on a bigger one. This keeps chunks close to a target size while preferring to break at natural boundaries (like paragraph ends) rather than mid-sentence.", "Semantic chunking uses embedding similarity to decide where to split: consecutive sentences are embedded, and a split point is inserted wherever the similarity between adjacent sentences drops sharply, on the theory that a sharp drop signals a topic change. Document-structure-aware chunking instead uses explicit structure already present in the source — markdown headers, HTML tags, PDF layout, or code function/class boundaries — to split along logical units the author already defined, which tends to produce the most coherent chunks when that structure is reliably present.

Chunk size itself is a trade-off along two axes. Larger chunks give the generator more surrounding context per retrieved chunk (fewer chances that a fact's necessary context got separated from the fact), but dilute the embedding: a long chunk covering several sub-topics gets one averaged embedding that may not closely match a query about any single sub-topic, hurting retrieval precision. Smaller chunks embed more precisely (an embedding of a focused, single-topic passage matches a focused query more closely) but risk fragmenting information that spans multiple sentences and increase the total number of vectors to index and search. A common mitigation is to embed and search over small chunks for precision, but expand each retrieved chunk to include its surrounding sentences or parent section before handing it to the generator, decoupling the unit of retrieval from the unit of context.", 'Having a large context window does not guarantee a model uses all of it equally well. Empirically, many long-context models exhibit a "lost in the middle" pattern: retrieval accuracy for a fact placed near the beginning or end of a long context is measurably higher than for the same fact placed in the middle, even though the fact is technically present and attention in principle allows access to any position. This means simply having a large enough context window to fit all potentially relevant documents is not sufficient for a system to reliably use all of them — a RAG system with poor retrieval that dumps twenty marginally-relevant chunks into a long context is not necessarily better, and can be worse, than one that retrieves three highly-relevant chunks, because the model may fail to weight the genuinely relevant one appropriately amid the noise.

This is one of the more important practical relationships between RAG and long-context models: a bigger context window changes how many retrieved chunks can fit, but it does not remove the value of good retrieval and ranking — it is generally more reliable to retrieve fewer, more precisely relevant chunks (helped by good chunking, hybrid search, and re-ranking) than to rely on a large context window to compensate for imprecise retrieval by including many chunks and hoping the model finds the right one.', '# Hybrid Search and Re-ranking

Hybrid search combines a sparse lexical method (typically BM25) with a dense semantic method (vector similarity over embeddings) into a single ranked result list, on the premise that the two methods have complementary strengths: BM25 is precise about exact terms but blind to paraphrase, while dense retrieval understands paraphrase and meaning but can miss queries that hinge on a specific rare term or identifier.

A document ranked highly by either method gets a large contribution; a document that both methods agree is relevant gets contributions from both lists and rises to the top. RRF requires no score normalization and no tuned weights, which makes it a robust default, though a weighted linear combination of min-max-normalized scores is a common alternative when there is enough labeled data to tune the weights.', 'Causal (masked) self-attention is used in autoregressive decoders: a mask sets the attention score from position i to any position j > i to negative infinity before the softmax, so a token can only attend to itself and earlier tokens. This enforces that the model cannot "look ahead" at tokens it is supposed to predict, which is essential for training decoder-only language models with teacher forcing and for correct behavior during generation.

Attention weights are sometimes used for interpretability, on the intuition that high attention from token A to token B means B was influential in producing A's representation. This intuition is not fully reliable in deep, multi-layer, multi-head models, because information is mixed across many layers and heads and the residual stream carries forward information that never gets explicitly "re-attended" to. Attention weights are best treated as one diagnostic signal among several, not as a complete causal explanation of model behavior.

Key-value (KV) caching is an inference-time optimization for autoregressive decoding: since causal attention means past keys and values never change as new tokens are generated, they can be computed once and cached, so each new token only requires computing attention against the cached K/V pairs rather than recomputing them for the whole sequence. This is what makes token-by-token generation with large decoder-only models tractable in production.']

user_input: What is the key limitation of prompt engineering as a model adaptation method?
retrieved_contexts:
["# Fine-Tuning, Prompt Engineering, and RAG: Choosing an Approach

There are three broad ways to adapt a pretrained language model to a specific task or knowledge domain, and they are not mutually exclusive: prompt engineering, retrieval-augmented generation, and fine-tuning. Choosing between them is a question of what kind of adaptation is actually needed — a new skill or behavior, versus new knowledge, versus a narrow output format — and each has a different cost profile.

Prompt engineering adapts model behavior purely through the text of the input at inference time: instructions, examples (few-shot prompting), and formatting requirements, with no change to the model's weights. It is the cheapest and fastest option to iterate on, requires no training infrastructure, and works within a single API call, but it is bounded by the context window and by what the base model is already capable of — a prompt cannot teach a model facts it was never exposed to, and very long, complex instructions can be inconsistently followed by weaker models.", "Retrieval-augmented generation adapts the model's effective knowledge without touching its weights, by supplying relevant external information in-context at query time, as covered in the RAG document. It is the natural choice when the task is fundamentally about answering questions over a specific, possibly large or frequently changing, body of knowledge — because that knowledge can be updated by re-indexing documents, with no retraining required, and answers can be grounded in retrievable, citable sources.

Fine-tuning updates the model's weights on a task-specific dataset, so the adaptation is baked into the model itself rather than supplied at inference time. It is the right tool when the goal is to change how the model behaves — its tone, its output format, its ability to follow a domain-specific instruction schema, or a narrow skill like structured extraction — rather than what it knows. Full fine-tuning updates all of a model's parameters and is expensive in compute and data; parameter-efficient fine-tuning methods such as LoRA (Low-Rank Adaptation) instead freeze the original weights and train small, low-rank update matrices injected into specific layers, dramatically reducing the number of trainable parameters and the memory needed, at some cost in achievable adaptation capacity compared to full fine-tuning.", 'The classic RLHF pipeline has three stages. First, supervised fine-tuning (SFT): the pretrained base model is fine-tuned on a smaller, high-quality dataset of example prompts and ideal responses, written or curated by humans, to establish a baseline instruction-following behavior. Second, reward model training: human annotators are shown multiple model outputs for the same prompt and rank them by preference; this preference data trains a separate reward model to predict a scalar score for how much a human would like any given response. Third, reinforcement learning: the SFT model is further optimized (commonly with an algorithm called PPO, Proximal Policy Optimization) to generate outputs that the reward model scores highly, while a penalty term (typically a KL-divergence constraint against the original SFT model) discourages the policy from drifting so far that it starts exploiting quirks of the reward model rather than genuinely improving — a failure mode known as reward hacking.', 'For large language models specifically, distillation commonly takes the form of using a large, expensive model to generate a large dataset of high-quality outputs (answers, chain-of-thought reasoning traces, or preference judgments) for a wide variety of prompts, and then fine-tuning a smaller model on that generated dataset with ordinary supervised fine-tuning — sometimes called "sequence-level" or "black-box" distillation, since it only requires access to the teacher's text outputs rather than its internal probability distributions or weights, which is important when the teacher is only available behind an API. This is the approach used to produce many small, capable open-weight models that closely imitate the style and, to a significant extent, the capability of a much larger closed model on similar prompts.

Distillation has practical limits: a small student model has fundamentally less capacity than a large teacher, so it cannot perfectly replicate the teacher's behavior on the hardest tasks in the teacher's distribution, and a student trained heavily on a teacher's outputs can inherit the teacher's specific errors, stylistic quirks, and blind spots just as reliably as it inherits its strengths. Distilled models also tend to generalize somewhat less well outside the specific distribution of prompts they were distilled on, compared to a model of similar size trained directly on diverse human-generated data, which is why distillation datasets are usually constructed to be broad and diverse rather than narrowly focused on a single task.', 'Several factors increase hallucination risk. Long-tail or rarely-seen facts during pretraining are more likely to be misremembered or fabricated than well-represented, frequently-repeated facts. user_input: What is the difference between a 'hard label' and a 'soft label' in Hinton et al.'s knowledge distillation formulation?
retrieved_contexts:
['The classic formulation of distillation, introduced by Hinton et al., trains the student not just to match the teacher's single top prediction (a "hard label") but to match the teacher's full output probability distribution over all possible outputs (a "soft label"). The intuition is that a teacher's probability distribution carries more information than its single most likely answer — if a teacher assigns 70% probability to "cat" and 25% to "dog" and 5% to everything else for a given image, that relative ranking and those relative magnitudes convey which mistakes are "reasonable" (confusing cat and dog) versus "unreasonable" (confusing cat and truck), information a single hard label throws away. A temperature parameter is used to soften the teacher's distribution (making the non-top probabilities larger and more informative) before computing the training loss against the student.', '# Knowledge Distillation

Knowledge distillation is a technique for training a smaller "student" model to reproduce the behavior of a larger, more capable "teacher" model, with the goal of retaining as much of the teacher's quality as possible in a model that is cheaper and faster to run. It is a distinct technique from quantization: quantization reduces the numerical precision of an existing model's weights, while distillation trains a genuinely smaller model (fewer parameters, and often a different architecture entirely) from scratch or from a smaller pretrained base, using the teacher's outputs as a training signal. The two are complementary and are often applied together — a distilled model can subsequently be quantized as well.', 'For large language models specifically, distillation commonly takes the form of using a large, expensive model to generate a large dataset of high-quality outputs (answers, chain-of-thought reasoning traces, or preference judgments) for a wide variety of prompts, and then fine-tuning a smaller model on that generated dataset with ordinary supervised fine-tuning — sometimes called "sequence-level" or "black-box" distillation, since it only requires access to the teacher's text outputs rather than its internal probability distributions or weights, which is important when the teacher is only available behind an API. This is the approach used to produce many small, capable open-weight models that closely imitate the style and, to a significant extent, the capability of a much larger closed model on similar prompts.

Distillation has practical limits: a small student model has fundamentally less capacity than a large teacher, so it cannot perfectly replicate the teacher's behavior on the hardest tasks in the teacher's distribution, and a student trained heavily on a teacher's outputs can inherit the teacher's specific errors, stylistic quirks, and blind spots just as reliably as it inherits its strengths. Distilled models also tend to generalize somewhat less well outside the specific distribution of prompts they were distilled on, compared to a model of similar size trained directly on diverse human-generated data, which is why distillation datasets are usually constructed to be broad and diverse rather than narrowly focused on a single task.', "# Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG)

Retrieval-Augmented Generation is an architecture that couples a language model with an external retrieval step: instead of relying solely on knowledge baked into the model's parameters during pretraining, the system first retrieves relevant passages from an external corpus and then conditions the model's generation on those retrieved passages, typically by inserting them into the prompt. The term was coined in a 2020 paper by Lewis et al., though the general idea of grounding generation in retrieved evidence predates that specific formulation.

RAG addresses three well-known weaknesses of relying on a language model's parametric knowledge alone. First, hallucination: a model asked about facts it never saw, or saw rarely, during training will often generate plausible-sounding but incorrect text rather than admitting uncertainty; grounding generation in retrieved source text gives the model something concrete to draw from and gives users a way to verify claims against a cited source. Second, staleness: a model's knowledge is frozen at its training cutoff, while a retrieval corpus can be updated continuously without retraining the model. Third, cost and specificity: fine-tuning a large model to memorize a narrow, proprietary, or frequently-changing document set is expensive and often unnecessary if the same documents can simply be retrieved at query time.", '# Hybrid Search and Re-ranking

Hybrid search combines a sparse lexical method (typically BM25) with a dense semantic method (vector similarity over embeddings) into a single ranked result list, on the premise that the two methods have complementary strengths: BM25 is precise about exact terms but blind to paraphrase, while dense retrieval understands paraphrase and meaning but can miss queries that hinge on a specific rare term or identifier.

The central challenge in hybrid search is that BM25 scores and cosine-similarity scores live on different, incomparable scales — a BM25 score might range from 0 to 30 depending on the corpus, while cosine similarity is bounded between -1 and 1 — so the two rankings cannot simply be summed. Reciprocal Rank Fusion (RRF) sidesteps this by ignoring the raw scores entirely and combining rankings instead: for each document, RRF computes 1 / (k + rank) in each ranked list it appears in (where k is a small constant, commonly 60, that dampens the influence of very low ranks) and sums this across lists. A document ranked highly by either method gets a large contribution; a document that both methods agree is relevant gets contributions from both lists and rises to the top. RRF requires no score normalization and no tuned weights, which makes it a robust default, though a weighted linear combination of min-max-normalized scores is a common alternative when there is enough labeled data to tune the weights.']

A language model's context window is the maximum number of tokens (a token being roughly a word-piece — a whole word, part of a word, or punctuation) it can process in a single forward pass, spanning both the input prompt and the tokens generated so far. Early Transformer LLMs had context windows of a few thousand tokens; modern frontier models commonly support context windows of 100,000 to over a million tokens, driven by both architectural changes and systems-level optimization, since naive self-attention's quadratic cost in sequence length made very long contexts computationally impractical in the original Transformer formulation.", "Extending context length has required progress on several fronts. retrieved_contexts:
["Extending context length has required progress on several fronts. Positional encoding schemes that generalize better to lengths unseen during training — such as RoPE (rotary position embeddings) combined with scaling techniques that stretch or reinterpret position indices at inference time — let a model trained at one context length process meaningfully longer sequences without retraining from scratch, though usually with some quality degradation the further the extrapolation goes. Efficient attention implementations, especially FlashAttention, reduce the memory bandwidth cost of computing exact attention by restructuring the computation to avoid materializing the full attention matrix in slow GPU memory, which does not change attention's quadratic compute cost but substantially reduces its practical memory and wall-clock cost. And architectural variants such as sliding-window attention (each token only attends to a fixed-size local window of nearby tokens in most layers) or various sparse/linear attention schemes trade some ability to model arbitrary long-range interactions for sub-quadratic (or even linear) scaling in sequence length.", '# Attention Mechanisms

Attention is a way for a model to compute a weighted combination of a set of values, where the weights are determined by how relevant each value is to a given query. In the scaled dot-product attention used by Transformers, every input token is projected into three vectors: a query (Q), a key (K), and a value (V). The attention score between a query and a key is their dot product, scaled by the square root of the key dimension to keep gradients stable, and then passed through a softmax so the scores for a given query sum to one. The output for that query is the weighted sum of all value vectors, using those softmax weights.

Self-attention is the special case where queries, keys, and values all come from the same sequence, so each token attends to every other token in that sequence, including itself. Cross-attention is the case where queries come from one sequence (for example, a decoder's partially generated output) and keys/values come from a different sequence (for example, an encoder's output), which is how encoder-decoder models condition generation on an input.

Multi-head attention splits the query, key, and value projections into several smaller subspaces ("heads"), runs scaled dot-product attention independently in each subspace, and concatenates the results. This lets the model attend to information from different representation subspaces at different positions simultaneously, rather than being forced to average all relevant signals into a single attention distribution per layer.', "Because self-attention has no inherent notion of token order, Transformers add positional information explicitly. The original paper used fixed sinusoidal positional encodings added to the input embeddings; later models introduced learned positional embeddings, relative position representations, and rotary position embeddings (RoPE), which encode position by rotating query and key vectors as a function of their position, improving extrapolation to longer sequences than seen during training.

The original architecture had an encoder stack and a decoder stack. The encoder produces contextualized representations of the input sequence, while the decoder generates output tokens autoregressively, attending both to previously generated tokens (via masked self-attention) and to the encoder's output (via cross-attention). Encoder-only models (like BERT) are well suited to understanding tasks such as classification and extraction, decoder-only models (like GPT-style LLMs) are well suited to open-ended generation, and encoder-decoder models (like T5) are used for sequence-to-sequence tasks such as translation and summarization.

The main computational cost of a Transformer is the self-attention operation, whose time and memory scale quadratically with sequence length because every token must be compared with every other token. This has motivated a large body of work on efficient attention variants (sparse attention, linear attention, sliding-window attention) and on systems-level optimizations such as FlashAttention, which restructures the attention computation to reduce memory reads and writes on the GPU without changing the mathematical result.", 'Causal (masked) self-attention is used in autoregressive decoders: a mask sets the attention score from position i to any position j > i to negative infinity before the softmax, so a token can only attend to itself and earlier tokens. This enforces that the model cannot "look ahead" at tokens it is supposed to predict, which is essential for training decoder-only language models with teacher forcing and for correct behavior during generation.

Attention weights are sometimes used for interpretability, on the intuition that high attention from token A to token B means B was influential in producing A's representation. This intuition is not fully reliable in deep, multi-layer, multi-head models, because information is mixed across many layers and heads and the residual stream carries forward information that never gets explicitly "re-attended" to. Attention weights are best treated as one diagnostic signal among several, not as a complete causal explanation of model behavior.

Key-value (KV) caching is an inference-time optimization for autoregressive decoding: since causal attention means past keys and values never change as new tokens are generated, they can be computed once and cached, so each new token only requires computing attention against the cached K/V pairs rather than recomputing them for the whole sequence. This is what makes token-by-token generation with large decoder-only models tractable in production.', "# Fine-Tuning, Prompt Engineering, and RAG: Choosing an Approach

There are three broad ways to adapt a pretrained language model to a specific task or knowledge domain, and they are not mutually exclusive: prompt engineering, retrieval-augmented generation, and fine-tuning. Choosing between them is a question of what kind of adaptation is actually needed — a new skill or behavior, versus new knowledge, versus a narrow output format — and each has a different cost profile.

Prompt engineering adapts model behavior purely through the text of the input at inference time: instructions, examples (few-shot prompting), and formatting requirements, with no change to the model's weights. It is the cheapest and fastest option to iterate on, requires no training infrastructure, and works within a single API call, but it is bounded by the context window and by what the base model is already capable of — a prompt cannot teach a model facts it was never exposed to, and very long, complex instructions can be inconsistently followed by weaker models."]

retrieved_contexts:
['Having a large context window does not guarantee a model uses all of it equally well. Empirically, many long-context models exhibit a "lost in the middle" pattern: retrieval accuracy for a fact placed near the beginning or end of a long context is measurably higher than for the same fact placed in the middle, even though the fact is technically present and attention in principle allows access to any position. This means simply having a large enough context window to fit all potentially relevant documents is not sufficient for a system to reliably use all of them — a RAG system with poor retrieval that dumps twenty marginally-relevant chunks into a long context is not necessarily better, and can be worse, than one that retrieves three highly-relevant chunks, because the model may fail to weight the genuinely relevant one appropriately amid the noise.

This is one of the more important practical relationships between RAG and long-context models: a bigger context window changes how many retrieved chunks can fit, but it does not remove the value of good retrieval and ranking — it is generally more reliable to retrieve fewer, more precisely relevant chunks (helped by good chunking, hybrid search, and re-ranking) than to rely on a large context window to compensate for imprecise retrieval by including many chunks and hoping the model finds the right one.', 'For RAG specifically, the RAGAS framework decomposes evaluation into metrics that isolate retrieval quality from generation quality, since a RAG system can fail at either stage independently. Context precision measures what fraction of the retrieved chunks are actually relevant to the question, penalizing a retriever that pads its results with irrelevant passages. Context recall measures whether the retrieved chunks, taken together, contain all the information present in a reference (ground-truth) answer, penalizing a retriever that missed something necessary. Faithfulness measures whether every claim in the generated answer is actually supported by the retrieved context, by decomposing the answer into individual claims and checking each one against the context — this specifically targets hallucination that happens even when relevant context was retrieved. Answer relevancy measures whether the generated answer actually addresses the question asked, independent of whether it is factually correct, catching cases where a model produces a well-supported but off-topic or evasive response.', "A typical RAG pipeline has an offline (indexing) path and an online (query) path. Offline, documents are split into chunks, each chunk is embedded, and the embeddings (plus the chunk text and metadata) are stored in a vector index. Online, an incoming query is embedded with the same model, the vector index returns the top-k most similar chunks, and those chunks are formatted into a prompt template along with the user's question and handed to the generator LLM, which produces an answer conditioned on that context.

The quality of a RAG system is bottlenecked by whichever stage performs worst: if retrieval fails to surface the passage that actually contains the answer, no amount of generation quality can recover, because the model was never given the right information. This is why RAG evaluation typically decomposes into retrieval metrics (did we find the right passages?) and generation metrics (given the passages we found, did the model produce a faithful, relevant answer?) rather than only scoring the final answer end-to-end.", "# Chunking Strategies for Retrieval

Chunking is the process of splitting source documents into smaller passages before embedding and indexing them, and it is one of the most under-appreciated levers in a RAG system's quality — even a perfect retriever and a perfect generator cannot produce a good answer if the relevant information was split across chunk boundaries in a way that neither chunk alone contains it.

Fixed-size chunking splits text every N tokens (or characters), optionally with an overlap between consecutive chunks so that content near a boundary still appears whole in at least one chunk. It is simple and predictable, and overlap (commonly 10-20% of the chunk size) directly mitigates the boundary problem, but fixed-size splitting is agnostic to the document's actual structure and can still cut a sentence or a table row in half.

Recursive character/token splitting improves on naive fixed-size splitting by trying a prioritized list of separators — paragraph breaks, then sentence breaks, then word breaks — recursively falling back to a smaller separator only when a chunk is still too large after splitting on a bigger one. This keeps chunks close to a target size while preferring to break at natural boundaries (like paragraph ends) rather than mid-sentence.", "# Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG)

Retrieval-Augmented Generation is an architecture that couples a language model with an external retrieval step: instead of relying solely on knowledge baked into the model's parameters during pretraining, the system first retrieves relevant passages from an external corpus and then conditions the model's generation on those retrieved passages, typically by inserting them into the prompt. The term was coined in a 2020 paper by Lewis et al., though the general idea of grounding generation in retrieved evidence predates that specific formulation.

RAG addresses three well-known weaknesses of relying on a language model's parametric knowledge alone. First, hallucination: a model asked about facts it never saw, or saw rarely, during training will often generate plausible-sounding but incorrect text rather than admitting uncertainty; grounding generation in retrieved source text gives the model something concrete to draw from and gives users a way to verify claims against a cited source. Second, staleness: a model's knowledge is frozen at its training cutoff, while a retrieval corpus can be updated continuously without retraining the model. Third, cost and specificity: fine-tuning a large model to memorize a narrow, proprietary, or frequently-changing document set is expensive and often unnecessary if the same documents can simply be retrieved at query time."]
response: The practical relationship between context window size and retrieval quality in a RAG system is that a larger context window alone does not necessarily improve performance if the retrieval is poor. The model may fail to weight genuinely relevant chunks appropriately amid irrelevant or marginally-relevant ones, even when many chunks are included due to a large context window. Therefore, good retrieval and ranking remain crucial, as relying on a large context window to compensate for imprecise retrieval can be less effective than retrieving fewer, more precisely relevant chunks.

BM25 (Best Matching 25) is a ranking function used to score how well a document matches a query, based on the query terms that literally appear in the document — it is a "sparse" or lexical method, in contrast to "dense" methods that compare learned embedding vectors. BM25 is a refinement of the older TF-IDF (term frequency–inverse document frequency) family: it scores a document highly if it contains the query's terms frequently (term frequency), especially if those terms are rare across the whole corpus (inverse document frequency, which downweights common words like "the" that appear everywhere and carry little discriminative signal).

BM25 improves on plain TF-IDF with two adjustments. First, it saturates term frequency: the tenth occurrence of a query term in a document adds much less score than the second occurrence, controlled by a parameter k1, reflecting the intuition that a document mentioning a term ten times is not necessarily ten times more relevant than one mentioning it once. Second, it normalizes for document length using a parameter b: without this, longer documents would score higher simply by containing more words and thus more chances to match query terms, so BM25 penalizes term matches in documents that are much longer than the corpus average.', '# Hybrid Search and Re-ranking

Hybrid search combines a sparse lexical method (typically BM25) with a dense semantic method (vector similarity over embeddings) into a single ranked result list, on the premise that the two methods have complementary strengths: BM25 is precise about exact terms but blind to paraphrase, while dense retrieval understands paraphrase and meaning but can miss queries that hinge on a specific rare term or identifier.

The central challenge in hybrid search is that BM25 scores and cosine-similarity scores live on different, incomparable scales — a BM25 score might range from 0 to 30 depending on the corpus, while cosine similarity is bounded between -1 and 1 — so the two rankings cannot simply be summed. Reciprocal Rank Fusion (RRF) sidesteps this by ignoring the raw scores entirely and combining rankings instead: for each document, RRF computes 1 / (k + rank) in each ranked list it appears in (where k is a small constant, commonly 60, that dampens the influence of very low ranks) and sums this across lists. A document ranked highly by either method gets a large contribution; a document that both methods agree is relevant gets contributions from both lists and rises to the top. RRF requires no score normalization and no tuned weights, which makes it a robust default, though a weighted linear combination of min-max-normalized scores is a common alternative when there is enough labeled data to tune the weights.', 'A common misconception is treating fine-tuning as a way to "teach the model new facts" as a substitute for retrieval: fine-tuning on a document corpus does tend to shift a model's outputs toward that corpus's style and can improve recall of frequently repeated facts, but it does not reliably give the model the ability to answer arbitrary questions about the corpus's long tail of specific details the way retrieval does, and it offers no way to cite a source or update a single fact without retraining.
